longForm.title: The Battle of Ia Drang Valley, 1965: The First Reckoning
longForm.excerpt: On 14 November 1965, the 1st Cavalry Division flew into a clearing in the Ia Drang Valley and landed in the middle of three PAVN battalions. What followed was the first major engagement of the Vietnam War — and the battle that let both sides believe, incorrectly, that they had found their winning strategy.
paragraphs: On the morning of 14 November 1965, Lieutenant Colonel Harold Moore ordered his 1st Battalion, 7th Cavalry Regiment into a clearing in the Ia Drang Valley that the Army's maps labeled Landing Zone X-Ray. The clearing was small — barely large enough to take eight Hueys at a time — and it sat at the base of the Chu Pong Massif, a mountain ridge running along the Cambodian border that US forces had not yet seriously contested. Moore had approximately 450 men. What the intelligence had not adequately conveyed, and what Moore discovered in the first thirty minutes, was that the Chu Pong Massif was occupied by three battalions of the People's Army of Vietnam's B3 Front: the 33rd and 66th Regiments, totaling nearly 2,000 soldiers who had been training specifically to engage American units at close range, eliminating the advantages of air support.

The engagement at LZ X-Ray lasted three days. The critical hours came on the afternoon of 14 November, when PAVN forces attacked the perimeter before Moore's full battalion had even landed. A platoon under Lieutenant Henry Herrick was cut off and surrounded; of the 29 men in the platoon, 8 were killed. The fighting across the perimeter was intense enough that at several points Moore ordered napalm dropped within 50 meters of his own lines. B-52 Arc Light strikes hit the Chu Pong ridge — the first use of strategic bombers in direct support of a ground engagement in Vietnam — but the strikes could not be called close enough to the perimeter to decisively affect the immediate battle. Moore's men held. By the time the 2nd Battalion, 5th Cavalry arrived to reinforce on 15 November, the PAVN assault had stalled, and the initiative shifted.

The battle's historiography has been complicated by the competing conclusions that the participants drew from it. Moore himself, in the memoir he co-wrote with journalist Joseph Galloway more than two decades later, presented X-Ray as a vindication of airmobile doctrine: the ability to concentrate combat power by helicopter at any point on the battlefield had worked, and the fighting qualities of the Air Assault infantry had held a perimeter that an earlier generation of soldiers, depending on ground transport, could not have reached. This reading was not wrong. But it was incomplete in ways that the subsequent conduct of the war would make clear.

General William Westmoreland, commanding Military Assistance Command Vietnam, drew a different conclusion, and the one he drew had larger strategic consequences. Westmoreland interpreted Ia Drang as confirmation of the attrition strategy: the United States had engaged a PAVN force, killed far more of them than it had lost, and driven the survivors back across the Cambodian border. By the arithmetic of the body count — which MACV was already using as the primary metric of progress — Ia Drang was a success. What this reading missed was the PAVN's own interpretation of the battle. Senior North Vietnamese commanders, including Major General Chu Huy Man who commanded the B3 Front, later recorded that Ia Drang had taught them the techniques for 'grab them by the belt' tactics: close engagement at distances that negated American firepower advantages. The battle that Westmoreland read as proof that attrition worked was simultaneously providing the enemy with the tactical manual for countering it.

The second battle of the Ia Drang campaign, fought four kilometers north at LZ Albany on 17 November, has received far less attention than X-Ray in American military histories, largely because its outcome was catastrophic. The 2nd Battalion, 7th Cavalry, marching in column through tall elephant grass toward the Albany clearing, was ambushed by elements of the 8th Battalion, 66th Regiment, which had been following the column at close range and attacked when it was strung out and unable to return effective fire. The PAVN assault hit the column simultaneously at multiple points. Soldiers were killed before they could identify where the fire was coming from. Of the approximately 500 men in the column, 155 were killed and 124 wounded — proportional casualties that exceeded many of the bloodiest engagements of the Korean War. The fight at Albany lasted into the night, with survivors forming small defensive perimeters in the grass.

The disparity between the attention given to X-Ray and Albany in American accounts of Ia Drang reflects something larger about how the United States processed the Vietnam War at the time. X-Ray was a story of difficult combat successfully concluded, of airmobile doctrine validated, of American soldiers holding their perimeter against numerical odds. Albany was a story of a column walking into an ambush that killed nearly a third of its strength, of the PAVN demonstrating that they could control the conditions of engagement even against a superior American force, of the night being lethal in ways that daylight and air support could not reliably address. The Army's official accounts of Ia Drang emphasized X-Ray. The families of the 155 men killed at Albany had a different relationship to the battle.

General Vo Nguyen Giap, in later interviews, described Ia Drang as an important learning experience rather than a defeat. The PAVN had fought American airmobile forces directly, had learned what those forces could and could not do, and had extricated the majority of the B3 Front intact across the Cambodian border — a border that American ground forces were not, at that point, permitted to cross. Whether Giap had intended to test the Americans or had been surprised by the ferocity of the encounter at X-Ray has been debated. What is clear from Vietnamese accounts is that the lessons drawn at Ia Drang were incorporated into PAVN training and doctrine within months, and that the engagement at LZ Albany was considered a significant PAVN tactical success.

The Ia Drang battles produced the casualty figures that Westmoreland reported to Washington as evidence that the strategy was working: 234 Americans killed against an estimated 634 PAVN dead at X-Ray alone, with much higher estimates for the wider campaign. The arithmetic looked favorable if the underlying assumption — that the North Vietnamese had a finite pool of will and manpower that could be exhausted — was correct. It was not correct. In the decade that followed, the United States would discover that the PAVN could replace its losses faster than the body count strategy could generate them, that Hanoi's political will was not subject to attrition in the way that Westmoreland's model required, and that the battle that had looked, in November 1965, like the beginning of a winning strategy was in fact the first indication of why that strategy would fail.

shortForm.title: LZ Albany, November 1965: The Battle That Was Not Reported
shortForm.excerpt: Four kilometers from LZ X-Ray, two days after Moore's battalion had held its perimeter, the 2nd Battalion, 7th Cavalry walked into an ambush that killed 155 men. Albany was the bloodier half of Ia Drang. It was also the half that the Army's public affairs operation preferred not to emphasize.
paragraphs: On 17 November 1965, the 2nd Battalion, 7th Cavalry, received orders to march from X-Ray to a new clearing designated LZ Albany, approximately four kilometers to the north. The column moved through tall elephant grass in single file. An element of the 8th Battalion, 66th PAVN Regiment had been following the American column at close range, waiting. The ambush was initiated simultaneously at multiple points along the column's length — a technique designed to fragment the force and prevent mutual support. Soldiers in the middle of the column were engaged from both sides at distances of less than thirty meters, with no ability to identify firing positions in the grass.

The engagement lasted through the afternoon and into the night. Of approximately 500 men in the column, 155 were killed and 124 wounded. Several small groups of survivors formed defensive perimeters and held through the night under intermittent attack; others were killed individually as they attempted to reach the Albany clearing. The Air Cavalry doctrine that had worked at X-Ray — concentrate, call in air support, hold the perimeter — had limited utility when the perimeter was the column itself, strung out across several hundred meters of elephant grass in the dark. Relief forces did not reach all survivor positions until 18 November.

The official Army history of Ia Drang, and much of the subsequent public reporting, focused on LZ X-Ray. Albany received less coverage in part because the story it told was more difficult: an American battalion, in column, had been attacked and had suffered casualties at a rate comparable to some of the worst engagements of the Pacific War. Moore and Galloway's 1992 memoir We Were Soldiers Once... And Young treated Albany with the seriousness it deserved, and the 2002 film adaptation depicted the ambush. But the operational lesson of Albany — that the PAVN could control the terms of engagement even against an airmobile force, and that American tactical superiority was not a constant — was one that MACV's attrition framework had difficulty accommodating.

The families of the 155 men killed at Albany received the same telegrams as the families of the 79 killed at X-Ray. The distinction between the battles mattered less to them than to the strategists constructing the narrative of Ia Drang as a validation of American doctrine. Both groups of dead had gone into the same valley in the same week. What differed was which battle fit the story that the Army needed to tell in November 1965, and which did not.

onThisDay.headline: Ohio National Guard Opens Fire on Students at Kent State University, Killing Four
onThisDay.summary: On 4 May 1970, members of the Ohio National Guard fired into a crowd of students at Kent State University who were protesting President Nixon's announcement of the US invasion of Cambodia. Four students were killed and nine wounded. The killings accelerated the collapse of domestic support for the Vietnam War and provoked a nationwide student strike at over 450 universities.
